title: About me
goal: Say who you are, where you're from, where you live and which languages you speak, and ask others the same.
intro:
Now that you can say hello, it's time to introduce yourself. You'll learn all the personal pronouns, the present tense of 'to be' (हूँ, है, हो, हैं) and the main question words.

You'll also learn some lifesaving phrases for a beginner: 'I didn't understand', 'please speak slowly' and 'what does this mean?'.

vocab.note: Spoken as 'ye' and often written ये in informal Hindi.
Spoken as 'vo' and often written वो in informal Hindi.
Some speakers (esp. in UP/Bihar) also use हम for 'I'.
Also the respectful 'he/she' (near). Plural of यह.
Also respectful 'he/she'. Spoken as 'vo' — ये/वो serve for singular and plural in speech.
Present: हूँ hūṃ, है hai, हो ho, हैं haiṃ
Comes AFTER the noun: दिल्ली से 'from Delhi'.
m · also हिंदुस्तान hindustān, and 'India' in everyday speech.
Formal; in speech also हिंदुस्तानी hindustānī or 'Indian'.
मेरी (before f. nouns), मेरे (m. pl). Full system in Unit 3.
m · also used as a filler: 'I mean…'

phrases.en: Where do you live? (to a man; to a woman: रहती rahtī)
I live in Delhi. (woman speaking; man: रहता rahtā)
I speak a little Hindi. (man speaking)
I didn't understand. (man; woman: समझी नहीं samjhī nahīṃ)
Please speak a bit more slowly.

phrases.native: इसको हिंदी में क्या कहते हैं?
phrases.roman: isko hindī meṃ kyā kahte haiṃ?
phrases.en: What do you call this in Hindi?
Who is that? (spoken: vo kaun hai?)

grammar.title: Pronouns and 'to be' (होना) in the present
grammar.body:
The present tense of होना 'to be' has only four forms. Learn them with their pronouns:

मैं **हूँ** *maiṃ hūṃ* — I am
तू **है** *tū hai* — you are (intimate)
यह / वह **है** *yah / vah hai* — he, she, it, this, that is
तुम **हो** *tum ho* — you are (familiar)
हम **हैं** *ham haiṃ* — we are
आप **हैं** *āp haiṃ* — you are (respectful)
ये / वे **हैं** *ye / ve haiṃ* — they are; he/she (respectful)

There is **no separate word for 'he' and 'she'**: यह/वह means both (यह for someone near, वह for someone further away or not present). Gender shows up instead in verbs and adjectives. For respect, a single person is referred to in the plural: वे हमारे टीचर हैं 'He is our teacher' (lit. 'they are').

To make a sentence negative put **नहीं** before the verb. In negative sentences हूँ/है/हैं are often dropped: मैं भारतीय नहीं (हूँ).

examples.en: They are Indian. / He is Indian. (respectful)

grammar.title: Question words
grammar.body:
Hindi question words mostly begin with **k-**: क्या *kyā* 'what', कौन *kaun* 'who', कहाँ *kahāṃ* 'where', कब *kab* 'when', क्यों *kyoṃ* 'why', कैसे *kaise* 'how', कौन-सा *kaun-sā* 'which'.

They **don't move to the front** of the sentence as in English. They sit where the answer would go — usually just before the verb:

आपका नाम **क्या** है? — Your name **what** is?
मेरा नाम **सारा** है। — My name **Sarah** is.

Remember: क्या at the very **start** of a sentence is not 'what' but a yes/no question marker: **क्या** आप हिंदी बोलते हैं? 'Do you speak Hindi?'

dialogue.title: On the train to Jaipur
dialogue.setting: Sarah, a British student, gets talking to Amit, who is sitting opposite her.

lines.speaker: Amit
lines.native: अरे वाह! आप हिंदी बोलती हैं?
lines.roman: are vāh! āp hindī boltī haiṃ?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: A little. I'm a student here.

lines.speaker: Amit
lines.native: बहुत अच्छा! मेरा नाम अमित है। आपका नाम क्या है?
lines.roman: bahut achchhā! merā nām Amit hai. āpkā nām kyā hai?
lines.en: Very good! My name is Amit. What's your name?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: मेरा नाम सारा है। आप कहाँ रहते हैं?
lines.roman: merā nām Sārā hai. āp kahāṃ rahte haiṃ?
lines.en: My name is Sarah. Where do you live?

lines.speaker: Amit
lines.native: मैं जयपुर में रहता हूँ, पर मैं लखनऊ से हूँ।
lines.roman: maiṃ Jaypur meṃ rahtā hūṃ, par maiṃ Lakhnaū se hūṃ.
lines.en: I live in Jaipur, but I'm from Lucknow.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: माफ़ कीजिए, मैं समझी नहीं। ज़रा धीरे बोलिए।
lines.roman: māf kījiye, maiṃ samjhī nahīṃ. zarā dhīre boliye.
lines.en: Sorry, I didn't understand. Please speak a little slower.

lines.speaker: Amit
lines.native: जी, ज़रूर। मैं जयपुर में रहता हूँ। जयपुर।
lines.roman: jī, zarūr. maiṃ Jaypur meṃ rahtā hūṃ. Jaypur.
lines.en: Of course. I live in Jaipur. Jaipur.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: अच्छा, जयपुर! मैं भी जयपुर जा रही हूँ।
lines.roman: achchhā, Jaypur! maiṃ bhī Jaypur jā rahī hūṃ.
lines.en: Oh, Jaipur! I'm going to Jaipur too.

culture: Indians often ask personal questions early — where you're from, whether you're married, what you do, even what you earn. It is friendly curiosity, not rudeness, and you can answer as much or as little as you like. A foreigner who speaks even a few words of Hindi gets a warm reaction (अरे वाह! 'oh wow!'). Many Indians are multilingual: someone in Jaipur might speak Marwari at home, Hindi in the market and English at work — so don't be surprised if people switch to English to 'help' you. Smile and carry on in Hindi: हिंदी में बोलिए, प्लीज़।
